title: Putting the AI-Driven Sell-Off in Perspective
summary: LPL Research explains that shifting AI spending expectations have fueled volatility, while history shows corrections are common, even in strong years.

# Putting the AI-Driven Sell-Off in Perspective


[LPL Research](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/lpl-research.html)


Last Updated: November 23, 2026


*Today's blog was written by Chris Fasciano, Chief Portfolio Strategist, LPL Financial.*


Market volatility has intensified over the past week as concerns have grown about the outlook for AI spending, the implications for global economic growth, and the potential impact on S&P 500 earnings expectations in 2026 and 2027.


It’s normal for investors to become concerned during periods of market volatility. They question their long-term objectives and whether they have more risk in their portfolios than they can tolerate. Those feelings are often amplified when markets react quickly to new information and uncertainty.


As Ben Graham famously observed, "In the short run, the market is a voting machine, but in the long run, it is a weighing machine." Over the last month, investors have clearly voted that the positive fundamentals that helped markets overcome inflation, tariffs, geopolitical tensions, and other headline risks may now be at risk themselves. However, history has illustrated that times like this can create opportunities for long-term investors where appropriate.


## What Has Changed in the AI Outlook?


Two major issues have impacted AI exposed stocks over the last month. The first occurred on Election Day, when Democrats won a majority in the Senate, the House, and key governorships across the country. Several of these changes in leadership at the state level occurred in areas where AI data center buildouts have been prevalent, such as Texas, Georgia, and Ohio. This led some investors to worry that projects could face delays or higher costs due to increased regulatory scrutiny.


Even if these concerns were to come to fruition, it is unlikely to change 2027 spending plans but could begin to have an impact in 2028.


The second event occurred when Nvidia’s (NVDA) CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned from the company. Not only has he been the leading advocate for the AI sector, under his leadership Nvidia has provided financing for customers and data center buildouts alike. Interim CEO Collette Kress indicated that Nvidia intends to be more selective regarding future investments and financing commitments. While the company remains committed to supporting strategic partners, investors interpreted the comments as a sign that financing conditions for some AI-related projects could become less favorable going forward. This too raises concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout.


Regardless of the ultimate outcome, the recent selloff serves as a reminder that even fundamentally driven bull markets experience periods of uncertainty and correction.


## Market Declines Are Not Unusual Even In the Best Years


Sell-offs never feel good, and emotions run high during periods of turmoil. But the magnitude of this correction and the speed at which it happened weren’t unprecedented.

The “A Historically Normal Drawdown” chart illustrates that over the last 46 years, the average S&P 500 drawdown in a year is 14%. Despite that occurrence, 35 of those years have ended with the index closing higher.


While every sell-off has its own catalyst, they often share a common theme: investors begin to question whether new developments could alter the outlook for economic growth and corporate earnings. Market participants have seen that happen several times over the last couple of years whether the catalyst was inflation, tariffs, war in the Middle East, or AI spending.


## Don’t Miss the Forest for the Trees


There is no doubt that AI companies are an important driver of recent market returns. Companies such as Microsoft (MSFT), Meta Platforms (META), Alphabet (GOOG/L), and Nvidia (NVDA) have had strong fundamentals and exceptional earnings growth. Investors have rightfully rewarded those companies. The S&P 500 has become top heavy with a significant weighting in the 10 biggest names. This has led to a market cap-weighted decline of over 11% from the all-time high set in early October.


But the index is made up of another 490 names. The equal weighted S&P 500, which removes the impact of the size of the company from the index weighting, has declined roughly 2% over the same period. The market isn't repricing the entire economy. It's repricing expectations around a relatively small number of AI-dependent stocks


While the largest AI-related companies have driven a significant share of recent market returns, their size has also magnified the impact of the recent pullback on capitalization-weighted indices. Investors with diversified allocations across sectors and styles may find that portfolio performance has been more resilient than headline index moves suggest.


History suggests that periods of uncertainty often feel most uncomfortable precisely when investors are being presented with compelling long-term opportunities. While no one can predict how the current AI debate will ultimately unfold, maintaining a diversified portfolio aligned with long-term objectives has historically been one of the most effective ways to navigate short-term volatility while remaining positioned for future growth.
